variants.title: Run the RLHF loop
variants.context: An RLHF system is a feedback loop. Supervised fine-tuning creates a capable baseline, preference collection produces a valid comparison signal, a reward model turns those comparisons into a scalar proxy, and policy optimization improves against that proxy while staying near a frozen reference.
variants.prompt: A team is planning its first alignment round for an assistant. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Collect comparisons under a rubric with randomized presentation and retained disagreement.
Improve the policy against that reward model while penalizing divergence from the frozen reference.
Fine-tune on high-quality demonstrations so the policy already follows instructions.
Train a scalar reward model to rank chosen responses above rejected ones and test it on held-out prompts.

variants.hint: Which stage has to produce a capable model before comparisons are worth collecting?
variants.explanation: Each stage creates the evidence the next stage consumes, so preference optimization starts from a policy that can already follow instructions.

variants.title: Run the RLHF loop
variants.context: An RLHF system is a feedback loop. Supervised fine-tuning creates a capable baseline, preference collection produces a valid comparison signal, a reward model turns those comparisons into a scalar proxy, and policy optimization improves against that proxy while staying near a frozen reference.
variants.prompt: A high-risk medical language slice has almost no coverage. Put the stages in order for the round that repairs it.

items.text: Collect targeted comparisons on that slice with an audited rubric and escalation path.
Re-run policy optimization only after the slice evidence exists, keeping the reference frozen.
Retrain the reward model and report ranking accuracy and calibration for that slice specifically.
Confirm the SFT baseline still handles the slice's instructions before blaming preference data.

variants.hint: Which stage is the missing evidence actually in?
variants.explanation: A coverage gap is a data problem, so the fix is deliberate collection on the slice rather than more optimization pressure.

variants.title: Run the RLHF loop
variants.context: An RLHF system is a feedback loop. Supervised fine-tuning creates a capable baseline, preference collection produces a valid comparison signal, a reward model turns those comparisons into a scalar proxy, and policy optimization improves against that proxy while staying near a frozen reference.
variants.prompt: Reward scores climb while independent human ratings fall. Put the recovery steps in order.

items.text: Add adversarial and counterfactual comparisons that expose the exploited pattern.
Resume bounded optimization and recheck independent human outcomes before any promotion.
Refresh the reward model on new policy samples, especially from the failing slices.
Pause optimization, because the policy has left the range where the reward model was validated.

variants.hint: What has to stop before new data can help?
variants.explanation: Rising reward with falling external quality is a stop signal, and the repair happens in the preference data before optimization resumes.

variants.title: Operate the release loop
variants.context: A release loop versions the SFT policy, prompts, preference data, rubric, reward model, reference policy, and evaluation suite together, promotes only after independent gates pass, ships a bounded canary, and rolls back to a known policy when a guardrail breaches.
variants.prompt: A candidate policy has finished optimization. Put the release steps in order.

items.text: Start a bounded canary and monitor external evaluator results, refusal and length distributions, and user outcomes.
Promote only after independent quality, safety, and capability gates pass overall and on predefined slices.
Version the SFT policy, prompt distribution, preference dataset, rubric, reward model, reference policy, and evaluation suite together.
Roll back to a known policy when a guardrail breaches, saving rollouts and evaluator evidence.

variants.hint: What has to be recorded before any gate result means anything?
variants.explanation: A release is reversible only when every artifact is versioned together, so the rollback target and the evidence trail both exist.

variants.title: Operate the release loop
variants.context: A release loop versions the SFT policy, prompts, preference data, rubric, reward model, reference policy, and evaluation suite together, promotes only after independent gates pass, ships a bounded canary, and rolls back to a known policy when a guardrail breaches.
variants.prompt: A canary shows response length climbing and complaints rising while aggregate reward looks healthy. Put the response in order.

items.text: Hold promotion, since a predefined slice signal has breached its guardrail.
Save the rollouts and evaluator evidence so the next collection round targets the observed failure.
Read the canary's refusal and length distributions next to the reward-versus-human disagreement.
Roll back to the previous known policy so users stop receiving the regressed behavior.

variants.hint: Unusual length beside a healthy reward is a specific warning.
variants.explanation: A rising score with falling external quality is a stop signal, and the saved evidence becomes the next round's targeted data.

variants.title: Operate the release loop
variants.context: A release loop versions the SFT policy, prompts, preference data, rubric, reward model, reference policy, and evaluation suite together, promotes only after independent gates pass, ships a bounded canary, and rolls back to a known policy when a guardrail breaches.
variants.prompt: A team wants to spend its annotation budget where it changes decisions. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Select candidates by disagreement, uncertainty, and high-impact slices rather than by volume.
Audit the selection policy itself for coverage bias before the labels are collected.
Collect the round, then recheck slice coverage and agreement before the reward model is refit.
Version the current rubric, prompt distribution, and reward model so selections are attributable.

variants.hint: Cheaper labeling is only cheaper when the selection is audited.
variants.explanation: Active learning reduces waste only when the selection policy is audited for coverage bias, otherwise it concentrates the same blind spot.

variants.title: Score the constrained objective
variants.context: The constrained objective maximizes expected reward minus beta times the KL divergence from the frozen reference policy. The KL term is a brake that keeps the policy near behavior where the reward model and the regression suite have evidence, not a safety proof.
variants.prompt: A rollout earns a reward-model score of 3.2 and its sequence-level KL from the frozen reference is 12.0. The penalty coefficient beta is 0.05. What is the value of the constrained objective?
variants.hint: The penalty is scaled by beta before it is subtracted.
variants.explanation: The objective is expected reward minus beta times KL, so the brake is proportional to how far the policy moved from the reference.

mistakes.feedback: That subtracts the raw KL and never applies the 0.05 coefficient.
That adds the penalty instead of subtracting it, which would reward divergence.

variants.title: Score the constrained objective
variants.context: The constrained objective maximizes expected reward minus beta times the KL divergence from the frozen reference policy. The KL term is a brake that keeps the policy near behavior where the reward model and the regression suite have evidence, not a safety proof.
variants.prompt: Candidate A earns reward 4.0 with KL 30.0 and candidate B earns reward 3.4 with KL 10.0, both under beta 0.05. How much higher is the better candidate's constrained objective than the other's?
variants.hint: Score both candidates first, then compare the two results.
variants.explanation: The penalty can reverse a raw reward ranking, which is exactly why the constrained objective and not the reward score decides.

mistakes.feedback: That compares raw reward scores and ignores the divergence penalty entirely.
That reports the better candidate's objective rather than its margin over the other.

variants.title: Score the constrained objective
variants.context: The constrained objective maximizes expected reward minus beta times the KL divergence from the frozen reference policy. The KL term is a brake that keeps the policy near behavior where the reward model and the regression suite have evidence, not a safety proof.
variants.prompt: Measured KL is above target, so a team raises beta from 0.05 to 0.25 and rescores a rollout with reward 5.0 and KL 24.0. What is the constrained objective at the new beta?
variants.hint: Recompute the penalty with the new coefficient before subtracting.
variants.explanation: Raising beta strengthens the brake, so a divergent rollout can score below zero and stop being attractive to the optimizer.

mistakes.feedback: That keeps the old 0.05 coefficient and reports the objective before the change.
That subtracts beta itself rather than beta multiplied by the KL divergence.

variants.title: Name the failure and its repair
variants.context: RLHF fails in three named ways. Reward hacking exploits the proxy, oversight bias comes from the rubric and annotation pool, and distribution shift grows as optimization succeeds and the policy leaves the pairs the reward model was trained on.
variants.prompt: Reward-model scores rise steadily, responses grow much longer, and independent human raters score the answers lower than last week. What is happening and what should the team do?
options: Oversight bias, so rebalance the annotator pool and rewrite the rubric first.
Distribution shift in prompts, so resample the prompt distribution from production traffic.
Reward hacking, so stop optimizing and add adversarial and counterfactual preference data.
optionFeedback: Oversight bias shows up as a systematically skewed rubric or pool, not as a score that climbs while quality drops.
Prompt resampling changes the inputs, but nothing here says the prompts stopped representing production.
Correct, a rising proxy score with falling external quality and unusual length is the proxy-exploitation signature.
variants.explanation: Treat a rising reward score paired with falling external quality, unusual length, or slice regressions as a stop signal.

variants.title: Name the failure and its repair
variants.context: RLHF fails in three named ways. Reward hacking exploits the proxy, oversight bias comes from the rubric and annotation pool, and distribution shift grows as optimization succeeds and the policy leaves the pairs the reward model was trained on.
variants.prompt: Annotator agreement is 91 percent, but the pool is drawn from one region and a minority need is consistently labeled as the rejected response. What is the diagnosis?
options: Reward hacking, since the policy has learned to satisfy a shortcut the raters like.
Reward-model underfitting, since a larger model would separate the two responses better.
Oversight bias, since the pool and rubric define what the system is optimized to value.
optionFeedback: No optimization behavior is described here, so the failure sits in the labels rather than in the policy.
More capacity would fit the same biased labels more sharply rather than correcting them.
Correct, high agreement on a narrow rubric still produces a systematically wrong reward model.
variants.hint: High agreement is not a universal quality score.
variants.explanation: Majority labels can erase a legitimate minority need, so agreement must be read with rubric audits and slice coverage.

variants.title: Name the failure and its repair
variants.context: RLHF fails in three named ways. Reward hacking exploits the proxy, oversight bias comes from the rubric and annotation pool, and distribution shift grows as optimization succeeds and the policy leaves the pairs the reward model was trained on.
variants.prompt: Held-out pairwise accuracy was strong at the start of the run, but the policy now produces response styles unlike any training pair and reward scores have become erratic. What is the leading explanation?
options: Insufficient rollout size, so the batch should be enlarged until the scores settle.
Distribution shift, so bound updates with KL and refresh preference data from new samples.
A broken pairwise loss, so the chosen and rejected responses should be re-checked for swaps.
optionFeedback: A larger batch reduces noise but does not give the reward model evidence about unfamiliar behavior.
Correct, a reward model can be accurate in-distribution and unreliable exactly where an aggressive policy searches.
A label swap would have hurt held-out accuracy from the beginning rather than only after the policy moved.
variants.hint: Where did the reward model's training pairs come from?
variants.explanation: As the policy moves it leaves the reward model's evidence, so bound the update and refresh preference data with new policy samples.

variants.title: Say what each stage learns
variants.context: Each stage of the pipeline learns a different thing, and confusing them is how teams expect one stage to repair another. A strong optimizer cannot fix biased labels, and a reward model cannot reliably score behavior it has never seen.
variants.prompt: Match each stage of the pipeline to what it actually learns.

pairs.label: Supervised fine-tuning
pairs.detail: Imitates the answer tokens of a preferred demonstration for a prompt

pairs.label: Preference collection
pairs.detail: Records which of two answers better meets the rubric, with no perfect target needed

pairs.label: Reward modeling
pairs.detail: Maps a prompt and response to a score that orders the pair as annotators did

pairs.label: Policy optimization
pairs.detail: Searches for behavior that raises the proxy, including behavior absent from demonstrations

variants.hint: Two stages consume answers, and two stages consume comparisons.
variants.explanation: Optimization quality is bounded by preference validity, reward-model generalization, and constrained updates, so no stage repairs the one before it.

variants.title: Say what each stage learns
variants.context: Each stage of the pipeline learns a different thing, and confusing them is how teams expect one stage to repair another. A strong optimizer cannot fix biased labels, and a reward model cannot reliably score behavior it has never seen.
variants.prompt: Match each method to the situation where it is the right choice.

pairs.label: SFT
pairs.detail: Demonstrations exist and the desired behavior is mostly imitation

pairs.label: DPO
pairs.detail: High-quality offline preference pairs fit the objective and simpler training is valuable

pairs.label: RLHF with online optimization
pairs.detail: Exploration against a validated reward signal justifies the systems cost

pairs.label: RLAIF
pairs.detail: Feedback coverage or critique candidates need to scale beyond human throughput

variants.hint: Ask what evidence the team already holds before asking which loop to run.
variants.explanation: Every method still has to define whose preferences count, where the signal generalizes, and how a release can be reversed.

variants.title: Say what each stage learns
variants.context: Each stage of the pipeline learns a different thing, and confusing them is how teams expect one stage to repair another. A strong optimizer cannot fix biased labels, and a reward model cannot reliably score behavior it has never seen.
variants.prompt: Match each control to the risk it is meant to bound.

pairs.label: Frozen reference policy
pairs.detail: Gives the KL penalty a fixed point so divergence stays measurable

pairs.label: Stored behavior log probabilities
pairs.detail: Keeps the probability ratio correct across optimization epochs

pairs.label: Independent human evaluation
pairs.detail: Checks intent with evidence the reward model did not produce

pairs.label: Slice coverage audit
pairs.detail: Exposes languages, domains, and risk levels the comparisons never reached

variants.hint: Each control exists because one specific thing can go wrong.
variants.explanation: The KL term is a brake and not a safety proof, so independent evaluators and coverage audits carry the risks it cannot.
